newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Mothers, babies held in Zaire hospital over fees.
newsitem.headline: Mothers, babies held in Zaire hospital over fees.

text.p: Seven women and eight new-born babies are being held in the maternity wing of a Zairean hospital by its one security guard until they pay for treatment they received.
"I have been kept here with my baby since I gave birth on the 23rd of July because I can't afford the bills," one of the mothers, 35-year-old Luwondio Mumbele, told Reuters.
The women, most of whom underwent emergency cesarian section at the crumbling King Baudoin Hospital outside Kinshasa, have been there for as long as three months.
Like all the other babies in the room who include a sickly pair of identical twin girls, Mumbele's tiny boy looked shrivelled and malnourished, lying beside her on a spring bed with no matress.

"My husband is unemployed and I have six more children back home," she said. "All of them go hungry while I am away because I am the only one who earns the bread in the family. It is the authorities who should help us pay."
Her family could not even afford the journey to visit her from their home in the other side of the sprawling capital.

Dr Jean Nicoise Muakiele, who is in charge of the maternity wing at the state-owned hospital, said each of the women owed the hospital between three and nine million zaire, equivalent to between $40 and $120.
The hospital was built in 1988 with money donated by Belgium. But when relations soured with the former colonial power shortly afterwards it was taken over by the Zairean state.
Muakiele said now that Zaire no longer subsidises his or any other hospital in the anarchic Central African country, the only money that comes in to cover costs is from patients.

"We take on these emergency cases for humanitarian reasons. But we have to recover the money eventually to prevent the hospital from closing down altogether. We are obliged to use unusual means to force the patients to find the money," he told Reuters.

In his own dilapidated office, Muakiele explained that before most of the women were sent to him they were squeezed dry of funds by private clinics, sometimes the only access Zaireans have to medical treatment.
But he said some of the women were at the hospital in bad faith, hoping they would eventually leave the hospital without paying up.
